tagline.text: A 560 m steel suspension footbridge over the Abra River

location.label: Location
location.text: Abra River between Poblacion and Sabnangan, Luba, Abra

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half a day to 2 days / 1 night

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland

children.text: This steel suspension footbridge, roughly 560 m long, links Poblacion and Barangay Sabnangan in Luba, Abra. Completed in 2002 and named after Senator Juan Flavier, it is presented as one of the longest suspension footbridges in Southeast Asia.

The Sabnangan Footbridge is a steel suspension footbridge in Luba, Abra, in the Cordillera Administrative Region of northern Philippines. It connects Poblacion, the town center of Luba, with Barangay Sabnangan across the river, at a spot where the Abra River once divided the two communities. Sources give its length as about
or at least
, so treat it as falling roughly within that range.
Construction began in 1998 and finished in 2002, and one blog says it was formally opened on May 1, 2002. It is also called the
Flavier Suspension Footbridge

in honor of Senator Juan Flavier, a physician from Abra who served as Secretary of Health (1992~1998). Many travel articles call it the longest suspension footbridge in the Philippines and in Southeast Asia, but that is not an officially verified record, so keep that in mind.

This is not a tourist-built attraction but an everyday bridge that locals cross daily. In the past, people crossed by bamboo raft, which became dangerous when the river rose in the rainy season; the bridge now lets them cross the river safely on foot. Upstream, a bamboo raft crossing still operates and can be seen as well.
Luba is a remote mountain town about

by road from Bangued, the provincial capital of Abra. Getting there takes time and public transport runs only twice a day, so it is not a casual sightseeing stop, but that is also its charm: it is uncrowded and offers a quiet look at local life, the river and the mountains. Before you go, get the municipal tourism office's contact details in Bangued and check road conditions and jeepney times by phone or messenger once to avoid a wasted trip. Luba had about 6,400 residents in the 2024 census, and it keeps the slow, quiet feel of a small mountain town.

Walking slowly across the long iron bridge over the river is the main event here. The bridge sways a little with each step and more in strong wind, so hold the rail and take your time. The deck is described as about 2 m wide and hung from steel cables. Stop for a moment in the middle to take in the view of the mountains and the river.

blocks.title: The path down to the river from Poblacion

children.text: To reach the bridge, follow the footpath behind the Luba police station down to the riverbank. It makes a short walk that shows village life up close, and a plaque dedicating the bridge to Senator Flavier is said to stand at the entrance. Locate the police station on a map app first so you do not lose your way. The path is not steep, but it can be muddy after rain.

A little upstream from the Sabnangan bridge, people still cross the Abra River by bamboo raft. It is run by the local government and is free, though it is customary to give the boatman a small donation.
A spring-fed lake on a mountaintop that can be reached by a trail from the bridge, where you can fish, swim and raft on emerald water. One travel guide describes a hike of about
2 hours
A multi-tiered waterfall with more than fifteen levels; a guide is advised if you want to climb to the upper tiers. The low entrance and guide fees make it one of the most popular trips in Luba.

blocks.title: Caungugan Cave and the pine forest

children.text: Caungugan Cave is an easy hike of about
1 hour
from the jump-off point, with stalagmites and an underground lake inside. The pine forest of Sitio Botot is known for cool air, views and camping.

items.title: One-day plan
items.subtitle: Focused on the bridge after arriving in Luba

children.text: Board the Luba jeepney at the terminal near Zone 5 in Bangued. It runs once in the morning and once in the afternoon.
Arrive in Luba and stop by the municipal tourism office to ask about current road conditions and whether you need a guide.
Contact a restaurant ahead of time for lunch. Many local eateries cook to order, so tell them your arrival time.
Go down the footpath behind the police station, cross the bridge to Sabnangan and come back. Allow about
1.5~2 hours
round trip including photos.
Rest for a while on the Sabnangan side and watch residents using the bridge. Ask people before you photograph them.
Walk to the bamboo raft crossing upstream, enjoy the river view and wrap up the day.
A day trip back to Bangued is not realistic. Because the jeepney runs only twice a day, we recommend spending one night in Luba.
Take the morning jeepney to Luba, cross the bridge and see the raft crossing. Rest at your lodging in the evening.
Climb Boni Falls with a guide. A guide can serve a group of up to five people.
Choose either Banaaw Lake or Caungugan Cave, and if you have time, look out over the pine forest at Botot.
The lake and cave routes involve long walks, so pick just one depending on your stamina and the weather.

Little is known about lodging in Luba, so ask the municipal tourism office to recommend a place to stay. One travel guide also suggests camping in the pine forest at Botot. Bangued has several hotels around Calaba, Zone 5 and the plaza, and one travel guide advises booking ahead because beds are limited.
A few local eateries in Luba are recommended in guides. Many cook to order, so it helps to tell them your arrival time in advance. Bring drinking water and snacks from Manila or Bangued.

Abra is known for natural dyes and handloom textiles. Some guides mention that you can buy handwoven cloth or hats as souvenirs on the way back to Bangued, but prices vary by shop, so check locally. In Luba, home-style local eateries are said to serve chicken and noodle dishes, but the menu may change from day to day.
The Bangued–Luba jeepney runs only twice a day, so confirm the time the day before and get to the terminal early.
Walk to the bridge along the footpath behind the police station. If you are unsure of the way, ask the municipal tourism office or a resident.
There is no shade on the bridge. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
Wear comfortable, non-slip sneakers. You will walk a long way.
In strong wind the bridge sways a lot. Hold the rail and walk slowly.
Check road conditions and whether you need a guide at the municipal tourism office first.
Bring cash for the raft and ferry, since small donations are customary.
Carry plenty of cash. It is a remote town, so do not count on cards or ATMs; withdraw money in Bangued beforehand.
In the rainy and typhoon seasons, the Bangued–Luba road and the river crossings may be cut off. Check the latest road conditions and advisories before you leave.
The Bangued–Luba road is seasonal, and some sections are closed to traffic during typhoons.
The bridge can be slippery when wet and it sways in the wind. Avoid putting too many people on it at once.
Many sources are old, so jeepney times, fares and contact details may have changed.
Length and size figures differ by source and are not official records.
It is a remote area with limited medical and phone coverage. Bring personal medicine and a power bank.
